r4a-spine-only-dispatch-really-works.title: Run a real spine-only crew end to end
r4a-spine-only-dispatch-really-works.imperative: THE DECISIVE ITEM. The whole change exists so a crew can be dispatched with --spine and no --handoff. Nothing in the branch proves that works: every test asserts on the argv build_crew_argv returns, which is a string-construction test, not a behaviour test. Build a tiny throwaway spine in a scratch dir with two trivial gates, dispatch a real crew at it with --spine and NO --handoff via run_crew.py --backend cli --model sonnet, and watch what the crew actually does. Does it call spine_status? Does it drive the spine to done? Does it flounder because the prompt names no task? Report what you saw, including the crew's own output. If the crew cannot work from the spine alone, that is a BLOCK regardless of how clean the code is.
r4a-spine-only-dispatch-really-works.finding: RAN ONE. Built a scratch gated spine (/tmp/r4a-probe/SCRATCH_SPINE.json, work-id epic-559/r4a-probe, two gates: g1-alpha with a command postcondition, g2-evidence-probe with a check:null precondition, a waivable check:null postcondition and an artifact postcondition) that names NO handoff and NO result document. Dispatched for real: `python scripts/run_crew.py --backend cli --model sonnet --work-id epic-559/r4a-probe --gate g0-probe --role implementer --worktree <this worktree> --spine /tmp/r4a-probe/SCRATCH_SPINE.json --result /tmp/r4a-probe/RESULT.md --root /tmp/r4a-probe` -- no --handoff. The crew did exactly what the change claims: called spine_status first, started g1-alpha, wrote out.txt containing ALPHA, advanced; attested p1, started g2, ran the evidence probe, advanced; engine now reports "DONE: no open items" and "LEASE released". Child exit code 0, ~56s. It did NOT flounder and it did NOT author a plan of its own. Notably it did this under the STALE installed /home/tommy/.claude/skills/constellation-implementer/SKILL.md (installed Aug 9, still the pre-change text telling a dispatched crew to build its own plan and claim a lease) -- so the spine-only prompt alone was strong enough to override contrary skill doctrine. The prompt-construction half of the change is proven behaviourally, not just as an argv string. The dispatch's COMPLETION accounting is a separate defect -- see appended item r4g.

r4b-settings-merge-or-replace.title: Does --settings replace the crew's other settings?
r4b-settings-merge-or-replace.imperative: build_crew_argv now appends --settings <inline JSON> to EVERY crew dispatch, including existing handoff dispatches. The docstring ASSERTS this 'merges with' the repo's .claude/settings.json and the worktree's project settings. That is an assumption, not a measurement, and if --settings replaces rather than merges, every crew silently loses the permission allows in .claude/settings.local.json and unrelated hooks (Stop / SessionStart / PostToolUse) stop firing. Determine the real semantics empirically against the installed claude binary. Say which it is and what the consequence is.
r4b-settings-merge-or-replace.finding: MEASURED, not read: --settings MERGES. Probe against the installed claude 2.1.227 in a scratch project (/tmp/r4b-probe) with its own .claude/settings.json. (1) Baseline, no --settings: project PreToolUse[Bash] and PostToolUse[Bash] hooks fired. (2) With the real crew_settings_json() blob passed inline: both project hooks still fired. (3) Project settings' `env` key (R4B_MARKER) still reached the crew's shell (echo printed project-settings-survived) with the inline blob present -- a non-hook key survives too. (4) Same-event SAME-matcher collision (inline PreToolUse[Bash] vs project PreToolUse[Bash]): BOTH hooks fired -- the arrays are additive, the inline one does not shadow the project one. (5) Corroborating: with --settings present claude still printed "Ignoring 1 permissions.allow entry from .claude/settings.json", proving it still read and processed the project file's permissions block. Consequence: the docstring's claim is correct; no crew loses .claude/settings.local.json allows or unrelated Stop/SessionStart/PostToolUse hooks. Separately noted (not caused by this change): this worktree is NOT in ~/.claude.json's trusted projects, so project permissions.allow is already ignored for every crew dispatched here regardless -- crews work only because --allowedTools is a CLI flag. NOT tested: settings precedence for a scalar key set in both places (e.g. model), since the crew blob sets no scalar key.

r4c-hook-fires-in-a-real-dispatch.title: Does the waive denial actually fire, and do attest/attach still work?
r4c-hook-fires-in-a-real-dispatch.imperative: The implementer verified the hook by piping fake JSON at the hook script standalone. That proves the script's logic, not that Claude Code invokes it, matches it to mcp__spine__spine_evidence, or honours a deny. In a real dispatched crew: (1) make it attempt a waive and show the denial with the ask-up message; (2) show attest and attach still succeed in that same run. Both halves matter -- a hook that denies everything would pass a waive-only test while breaking every crew.
r4c-hook-fires-in-a-real-dispatch.finding: BOTH HALVES PROVEN IN THE REAL DISPATCH ABOVE, not by piping JSON at the script. (1) DENY: the probe spine's g2 c1 was deliberately made waivable (override_policy.allowed=true, reason_required=true) so the ENGINE would have granted the waive -- meaning any refusal can only come from the hook. The crew's own report (/tmp/r4a-probe/probe_report.txt, written by the crew) records under "WAIVE ATTEMPT" the verbatim text: "A crew must not waive its own bound spine check -- always ask up. Call spine_halt with action=block, name what you cannot satisfy, and return; only a human or commander waives it from there." That is WAIVE_DENY_REASON byte for byte, so Claude Code did invoke the hook, did match it to mcp__spine__spine_evidence, and did honour permissionDecision=deny. (2) NOT A BLANKET DENY: in that same run, on that same tool, `attest` succeeded twice ("attested g2-evidence-probe.p1", "attested g2-evidence-probe.c1") and `attach` succeeded ("attached e-g2-evidence-probe-1 (review-result) to g2-evidence-probe"), and the spine reached DONE -- which it could not have if the hook denied everything. The crew also read the denial as intended: it recorded the ask-up path and continued rather than treating it as a dead end. Independently corroborated by the spine's own journal/state (engine `current` reports DONE with the evidence attached). NOT tested: whether a crew that genuinely cannot satisfy a check actually calls spine_halt (the probe told it to continue).

r4d-python3-hardcoded.title: The hook command hardcodes python3
r4d-python3-hardcoded.imperative: crew_settings_json emits the literal command `python3 -c '<script>'`. The repo has an explicit open problem about hardcoded interpreters (#539, with #553 alongside) and a real resolution mechanism -- install_constellation.py probes ('py','python3','python') and writes an interpreter.json sidecar. A hardcoded python3 in a shipped launcher is the same defect that has already bitten this repo more than once, and it fails on a machine where python3 is not the name. Judge how serious this is here, whether it should block, and what the smallest correct fix is. Note that the human has ruled such hardcoding is acceptable short-term ONLY if recorded against #539.
r4d-python3-hardcoded.finding: IT BLOCKS, and it is worse than a portability nit because PreToolUse hooks FAIL OPEN. Measured: I ran claude -p with an inline --settings PreToolUse hook whose command was `python3-does-not-exist-r4f -c foo`; the Bash tool call proceeded normally (Output: hello-FAILOPEN), no error, no denial. Same with a hook that exits 0 printing non-JSON. So on any host where `python3` is not the interpreter name -- Windows with only the `py` launcher, or a box with only `python` -- the hook silently does nothing and the crew CAN waive its own bound spine check. The human's ruling ("agent cannot waive itself ... always ask up") is then unenforced with no signal at all, which is precisely the "no hidden fallback / fail visibly" posture in global-everyone.md. The repo already knows this: scripts/install_constellation.py::build_hook_command's docstring says, of a hook command's interpreter, "comes from the run's single resolve_interpreter() probe -- never re-probed here, never HARDCODED ... no single interpreter name works on every platform, which is why the git-tracked settings.json names none (#539)." crew_settings_json does exactly the forbidden thing, in a git-tracked file, for a hook command. And the human's short-term allowance does not apply: #539/#553 are NOT recorded anywhere in this diff -- `git diff main...HEAD | grep 539` finds nothing -- so the one condition attached to the allowance is unmet. SMALLEST CORRECT FIX: run_crew.py is itself a running Python process, so it does not need the installer's probe at all -- emit `shlex.quote(sys.executable)` (or `Path(sys.executable).as_posix()` quoted) instead of the literal `python3`. That is one line, needs no sidecar, and is correct by construction on every platform, since the interpreter that launched the launcher is by definition present. If the team prefers the existing machinery, resolve_interpreter()/interpreter.json is the alternative. Either way, add a test that the emitted command's argv[0] is not the literal string "python3".

r4f-shell-quoting.title: Attack the inline hook command's quoting
r4f-shell-quoting.imperative: The hook is a multi-line python program embedded inside a single-quoted shell string, with an assert guarding apostrophes in one interpolated constant. Try to break it: does the emitted command survive being parsed by whatever actually runs it? Does the assert cover every interpolated value or only WAIVE_DENY_REASON? What happens on a shell where single-quote semantics differ, or if the hook runner does not use a shell at all?
r4f-shell-quoting.finding: ATTACKED IT, three separate weaknesses; the quoting itself is correct on POSIX and wrong off it. (1) POSIX: sound. shlex.split(cmd) yields exactly 3 args (python3, -c, <program>) and the extracted program compiles as Python; the real dispatch in r4a proves a real shell runs it. (2) NON-POSIX: broken. shlex.split(cmd, posix=False) leaves argv[2] as "'import json,sys\n...'" with the single quotes NOT stripped -- cmd.exe treats a single quote as an ordinary character, so python would receive a program whose first character is an apostrophe and die on a SyntaxError. Combined with the fail-open behaviour I measured under r4d, the denial silently vanishes rather than erroring. The repo's own .claude/settings.json sets "shell": "bash" on every one of its four hook entries; crew_settings_json emits {"type","command"} with no "shell" key, so it does not even get the repo's own standing answer to this hazard. Adding "shell": "bash" is the cheapest half of the fix. (3) THE ASSERT COVERS THE RIGHT VALUE BUT IS THE WRONG MECHANISM. WAIVE_DENY_REASON is genuinely the only interpolated value -- _WAIVE_HOOK_PY's other literals use double quotes only, and json.dumps of the reason emits double quotes -- so today the coverage is complete (verified: no single quote anywhere in the emitted program). But it is a bare `assert`, which python -O strips: I confirmed `python -O -c "import run_crew"` runs with __debug__ False, so under -O a future apostrophe in that constant would emit a silently malformed command that, per (2)+fail-open, allows the waive. The repo already ships assert_shell_safe_command() in install_constellation.py for exactly this job; use that (it raises, it is not an assert) rather than a stripped-at-runtime assert. NOT tested: an actual Windows host -- I have none here, so (2) is a parse-level demonstration plus the repo's own documented Windows posture (references/windows.md, the `py` launcher recipes, the engine's no-posix-shell refusal), not an observed Windows failure.

r4g-spine-only-dispatch-always-reports-f.title: A spine-only crew that fully succeeds is still recorded `failed`
r4g-spine-only-dispatch-always-reports-f.imperative: Discovered while running r4a. The change made the crew's INPUT the spine instead of a document, but left the crew's COMPLETION contract as a document. `--result` is still hard-required for every launch (the `missing` list is work_id/gate/role/result), and `CrewBackend.verify` decides `completed` vs `failed` purely on that result artifact existing AND being fresh. The spine-only prompt never mentions a result artifact at all -- it says only "drive it gate by gate ... until it reports done", where the handoff prompt says "The run is only complete when the result artifact the handoff names exists". Determine whether a perfectly-executed spine-only crew is therefore always recorded failed, and whether any test on the branch covers it.
r4g-spine-only-dispatch-always-reports-f.finding: CONFIRMED BY THE r4a RUN, AND IT IS THE ONE REAL DEFECT I FOUND. My spine-only crew drove its spine to DONE and released the lease, child exit code 0 -- and run_crew.py printed `crew constellation/epic-559/r4a-probe/g0-probe/implementer/attempt-1 -> failed`. The registry entry records status "failed", result_present false, result_fresh false. Mechanism: the change moved the crew's INPUT from a document to the spine but left its COMPLETION contract as a document. That is r4g, and it is the authoring-side twin of the rule the reviewer is asked to apply. (2) global-everyone.md "no hidden fallback; fail visibly." The waive denial rides on a hook whose interpreter is hardcoded `python3`, and I measured that PreToolUse hooks fail OPEN (a missing interpreter lets the tool call through silently). Also: assert_shell_safe_command() already exists for the quoting guard, and a bare `assert` was used instead -- stripped under python -O, which I confirmed.

r4d-python3-hardcoded: IT BLOCKS, and it is worse than a portability nit because PreToolUse hooks FAIL OPEN. Measured: I ran claude -p with an inline --settings PreToolUse hook whose command was `python3-does-not-exist-r4f -c foo`; the Bash tool call proceeded normally (Output: hello-FAILOPEN), no error, no denial. Same with a hook that exits 0 printing non-JSON. So on any host where `python3` is not the interpreter name -- Windows with only the `py` launcher, or a box with only `python` -- the hook silently does nothing and the crew CAN waive its own bound spine check. The human's ruling ("agent cannot waive itself ... always ask up") is then unenforced with no signal at all, which is precisely the "no hidden fallback / fail visibly" posture in global-everyone.md. The repo already knows this: scripts/install_constellation.py::build_hook_command's docstring says, of a hook command's interpreter, "comes from the run's single resolve_interpreter() probe -- never re-probed here, never HARDCODED ... no single interpreter name works on every platform, which is why the git-tracked settings.json names none (#539)." crew_settings_json does exactly the forbidden thing, in a git-tracked file, for a hook command. And the human's short-term allowance does not apply: #539/#553 are NOT recorded anywhere in this diff -- `git diff main...HEAD | grep 539` finds nothing -- so the one condition attached to the allowance is unmet. SMALLEST CORRECT FIX: run_crew.py is itself a running Python process, so it does not need the installer's probe at all -- emit `shlex.quote(sys.executable)` (or `Path(sys.executable).as_posix()` quoted) instead of the literal `python3`. That is one line, needs no sidecar, and is correct by construction on every platform, since the interpreter that launched the launcher is by definition present. If the team prefers the existing machinery, resolve_interpreter()/interpreter.json is the alternative. Either way, add a test that the emitted command's argv[0] is not the literal string "python3".

r4f-shell-quoting: ATTACKED IT, three separate weaknesses; the quoting itself is correct on POSIX and wrong off it. (1) POSIX: sound. shlex.split(cmd) yields exactly 3 args (python3, -c, <program>) and the extracted program compiles as Python; the real dispatch in r4a proves a real shell runs it. (2) NON-POSIX: broken. shlex.split(cmd, posix=False) leaves argv[2] as "'import json,sys\n...'" with the single quotes NOT stripped -- cmd.exe treats a single quote as an ordinary character, so python would receive a program whose first character is an apostrophe and die on a SyntaxError. Combined with the fail-open behaviour I measured under r4d, the denial silently vanishes rather than erroring. The repo's own .claude/settings.json sets "shell": "bash" on every one of its four hook entries; crew_settings_json emits {"type","command"} with no "shell" key, so it does not even get the repo's own standing answer to this hazard. Adding "shell": "bash" is the cheapest half of the fix. (3) THE ASSERT COVERS THE RIGHT VALUE BUT IS THE WRONG MECHANISM. WAIVE_DENY_REASON is genuinely the only interpolated value -- _WAIVE_HOOK_PY's other literals use double quotes only, and json.dumps of the reason emits double quotes -- so today the coverage is complete (verified: no single quote anywhere in the emitted program). But it is a bare `assert`, which python -O strips: I confirmed `python -O -c "import run_crew"` runs with __debug__ False, so under -O a future apostrophe in that constant would emit a silently malformed command that, per (2)+fail-open, allows the waive. The repo already ships assert_shell_safe_command() in install_constellation.py for exactly this job; use that (it raises, it is not an assert) rather than a stripped-at-runtime assert. NOT tested: an actual Windows host -- I have none here, so (2) is a parse-level demonstration plus the repo's own documented Windows posture (references/windows.md, the `py` launcher recipes, the engine's no-posix-shell refusal), not an observed Windows failure.

consolidation.summary: BLOCK. The design is right and the core claim is real -- I dispatched an actual spine-only crew (no --handoff) and it called spine_status, drove a scratch two-gate spine to done, and released the lease, all while reading an INSTALLED SKILL.md that still tells it to author its own plan. The waive denial fires in a real dispatch with the exact ask-up message, and attest/attach still work in that same run. --settings measurably MERGES (project env key, project hooks, and even a same-matcher PreToolUse hook all survive), so no crew loses its other settings. Three things block. (1) r4g, found by running it: the change moved a crew's INPUT to the spine but left its COMPLETION contract a document -- --result is still hard-required and CrewBackend.verify judges on that artifact, while the spine-only prompt never mentions one, so my perfectly-successful crew was recorded `failed`. The one test named for this passes only because fake_launch writes the artifact the real crew is never told to write. (2) r4d/r4f: the denial hook hardcodes `python3` and I measured that PreToolUse hooks FAIL OPEN -- on a non-python3 host (or any non-POSIX shell, where the single-quoted program is not unquoted) the human's "an agent cannot waive itself" ruling is silently unenforced. install_constellation.py::build_hook_command's own docstring forbids exactly this ("never hardcoded ... which is why the git-tracked settings.json names none (#539)"), the repo's own hooks all set "shell": "bash", assert_shell_safe_command already exists, and #539 is not recorded anywhere in the diff -- so the human's short-term allowance does not apply. (3) r3/r4-quality: both behavioural claims were evidenced by string-matching generated agent-facing text, which global-crew.md names as not-evidence. Nothing else is wrong: scope held on every no-go, the deleted pins in test_mcp_adoption.py were genuinely obsoleted and the replacement goes red under mutation, the suite reproduces at 2548 passed / 1 skipped and the TDD red at 14 failed -> 112 passed, and the map is honestly regenerated. Fixes are small: name the result artifact in the spine prompt (or judge a spine-only crew on its spine reaching terminal), emit sys.executable instead of `python3`, add "shell": "bash", swap the stripped assert for assert_shell_safe_command -- and cover each with a test that does not fake its own precondition.
